claim: Resident microbes play important roles in the development of the gastrointestinal tract.
source: Resident microbes play important roles in the development of the gastrointestinal tract, but their influence on other digestive organs is less well explored.
evidence: Supported by established scientific consensus about microbiota-host interactions in gastrointestinal development.

claim: The normal expansion of the pancreatic β cell population during early larval development requires the intestinal microbiota.
source: Using the gnotobiotic zebrafish, we discovered that the normal expansion of the pancreatic β cell population during early larval development requires the intestinal microbiota and that specific bacterial members can restore normal β cell numbers.
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing germ-free and conventionally reared zebrafish.

claim: Specific bacterial members can restore normal β cell numbers in germ-free zebrafish.
source: Using the gnotobiotic zebrafish, we discovered that the normal expansion of the pancreatic β cell population during early larval development requires the intestinal microbiota and that specific bacterial members can restore normal β cell numbers.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing bacterial mono-associations restore β cell numbers.

claim: BefA is a previously undescribed protein that is sufficient to induce β cell proliferation in developing zebrafish larvae.
source: These bacteria share a gene that encodes a previously undescribed protein, named herein BefA (β Cell Expansion Factor A), which is sufficient to induce β cell proliferation in developing zebrafish larvae.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing purified BefA protein induces β cell proliferation.

claim: Homologs of BefA are present in several human-associated bacterial species.
source: Homologs of BefA are present in several human-associated bacterial species, and we show that they have conserved capacity to stimulate β cell proliferation in larval zebrafish.
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis and database searches identifying BefA homologs.

claim: BefA homologs from human-associated bacteria have conserved capacity to stimulate β cell proliferation in larval zebrafish.
source: Homologs of BefA are present in several human-associated bacterial species, and we show that they have conserved capacity to stimulate β cell proliferation in larval zebrafish.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing Enterococcus gallinarum and Enterobacter aerogenes homologs induce β cell expansion.

claim: Low diversity childhood fecal microbiota is associated with increased diabetes risk.
source: Our findings highlight a role for the microbiota in early pancreatic β cell development and suggest a possible basis for the association between low diversity childhood fecal microbiota and increased diabetes risk.
evidence: Supported by inference from the experimental findings and existing literature on microbiota and diabetes.

claim: Resident microbes promote epithelial differentiation in the developing zebrafish intestine.
source: Using the gnotobiotic zebrafish model, our group has shown previously that resident microbes promote host processes in the developing intestine such as epithelial differentiation (Bates et al., 2006) and proliferation (Cheesman et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by Bates et al., 2006.

claim: Resident microbes promote epithelial proliferation in the developing zebrafish intestine.
source: Using the gnotobiotic zebrafish model, our group has shown previously that resident microbes promote host processes in the developing intestine such as epithelial differentiation (Bates et al., 2006) and proliferation (Cheesman et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by Cheesman et al., 2011.

claim: Many diseases in peripheral digestive organs are correlated with microbial dysbiosis.
source: The role of microbes in the development of other digestive organs remains underexplored, despite the fact that many diseases in peripheral digestive organs are correlated with microbial dysbiosis (Chang and Lin, 2016; Gülden et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chang and Lin, 2016 and Gülden et al., 2015.

claim: The zebrafish has a well-characterized program of β cell development that is highly conserved with that of mammals.
source: The zebrafish has a well-characterized program of β cell development, which is highly conserved with that of mammals (Kinkel and Prince, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kinkel and Prince, 2009.

claim: Initial β cells in zebrafish embryos arise from precursors within the dorsal and ventral pancreatic buds.
source: In the zebrafish embryo, initial β cells arise from precursors within the dorsal and ventral pancreatic buds (Biemar et al., 2001; Field et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Biemar et al., 2001; Field et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2011.

claim: The dorsal and ventral pancreatic buds fuse by 52 hours post fertilization in zebrafish.
source: The two buds fuse by 52 hr post fertilization (hpf), and give rise to the fully fated pancreas with only a single islet of hormone-secreting endocrine cells, by 3 days post fertilization (dpf) (Biemar et al., 2001; Field et al., 2003; Kumar, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Biemar et al., 2001; Field et al., 2003; Kumar, 2003.

claim: The zebrafish pancreas has a single islet of hormone-secreting endocrine cells by 3 days post fertilization.
source: The two buds fuse by 52 hr post fertilization (hpf), and give rise to the fully fated pancreas with only a single islet of hormone-secreting endocrine cells, by 3 days post fertilization (dpf) (Biemar et al., 2001; Field et al., 2003; Kumar, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Biemar et al., 2001; Field et al., 2003; Kumar, 2003.

claim: Newly fated β cells begin to expand coinciding with larval emergence from the chorion by 3 dpf.
source: Coinciding with the approximate time of larval emergence from the chorion by 3 dpf, these newly fated β cells begin to expand (Chung et al., 2010; Dong et al., 2007; Hesselson et al., 2009; Kimmel et al., 2011; Moro et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chung et al., 2010; Dong et al., 2007; Hesselson et al., 2009; Kimmel et al., 2011; Moro et al., 2009.

claim: β cells derived from the dorsal bud become quiescent in zebrafish larvae.
source: β cells derived from the dorsal bud become quiescent, while ventral bud derived β cells begin to undergo expansion via mechanisms of both proliferation and neogenesis (Hesselson et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hesselson et al., 2009.

claim: Ventral bud derived β cells undergo expansion via mechanisms of both proliferation and neogenesis in zebrafish larvae.
source: β cells derived from the dorsal bud become quiescent, while ventral bud derived β cells begin to undergo expansion via mechanisms of both proliferation and neogenesis (Hesselson et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hesselson et al., 2009.

claim: The number of β cells within the primary islet almost doubles between 3 and 6 dpf in zebrafish.
source: Between 3 and 6 dpf, the number of β cells within the primary islet will almost double (Moro et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Moro et al., 2009.

claim: Intestinal colonization with microbes occurs concurrently with the early larval period of β cell expansion in zebrafish.
source: Intestinal colonization with microbes occurs concurrently with this early larval period of β cell expansion.
evidence: Supported by inference from developmental timeline and established knowledge of zebrafish development.

claim: The intestine of the emergent zebrafish larva becomes open to the environment at both the mouth and the vent by 3.5 dpf.
source: Following development of the gut tube within the sterile embryo, the intestine of the emergent larva becomes open to the environment at both the mouth and the vent by 3.5 dpf, allowing for inoculation by environmental microbes (Bates et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bates et al., 2006.

claim: A single bacterial species in mono-association can reach luminal carrying capacity within several hours in the larval zebrafish gut.
source: Within the larval gut, bacteria proliferate rapidly, such that a single species in mono-association can reach the luminal carrying capacity within several hours (Jemielita et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jemielita et al., 2014.

claim: Human post-natal β cell expansion occurs concurrently with intestinal tract colonization by commensal microbes.
source: Human post-natal β cell expansion also occurs concurrently with intestinal tract colonization by commensal microbes.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge of human development.

claim: In utero, human β cells are produced via differentiation from progenitors.
source: In utero, β cells are produced via differentiation from progenitors (Georgia et al., 2006; Stanger et al., 2007) and at birth this newly fated cell population begins to expand by self-proliferation (Georgia and Bhushan, 2004; Gregg et al., 2012; Kassem et al., 2000; Teta et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Georgia et al., 2006; Stanger et al., 2007.

claim: At birth, the newly fated human β cell population begins to expand by self-proliferation.
source: In utero, β cells are produced via differentiation from progenitors (Georgia et al., 2006; Stanger et al., 2007) and at birth this newly fated cell population begins to expand by self-proliferation (Georgia and Bhushan, 2004; Gregg et al., 2012; Kassem et al., 2000; Teta et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Georgia and Bhushan, 2004; Gregg et al., 2012; Kassem et al., 2000; Teta et al., 2007.

claim: Human β cell proliferation rates peak at 2 years of age and then steadily decline.
source: β cell proliferation rates peak at 2 years of age and then steadily decline (Gregg et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gregg et al., 2012.

claim: By 5 years of age, most of the human β cell mass has become slow cycling.
source: By 5 years of age, most of the β cell mass has become slow cycling and will not expand significantly again unless stimulated by elevated metabolic demands, such as obesity or pregnancy.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge of human β cell development.

claim: At birth, infants are exposed to their mothers' vaginal, fecal and skin associated microbes.
source: At birth, infants are exposed to their mothers' vaginal, fecal and skin associated microbes, which immediately begin to colonize the neonatal intestine (Biasucci et al., 2010; Dominguez-Bello et al., 2010; Palmer et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Biasucci et al., 2010; Dominguez-Bello et al., 2010; Palmer et al., 2007.

claim: By 3 years of age, the composition and complexity of the human microbiota typically resembles that of an adult associated community.
source: By 3 years of age, the composition and complexity of the microbiota typically resembles that of an adult associated community (Murgas Torrazza and Neu, 2011; Palmer et al., 2007; Yatsunenko et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Murgas Torrazza and Neu, 2011; Palmer et al., 2007; Yatsunenko et al., 2012.

claim: Factors such as diet, birth mode and antibiotic exposure can result in reduced microbial taxonomic diversity during early years of life.
source: However, factors such as diet, birth mode and antibiotic exposure can result in reduced microbial taxonomic diversity during these early years of life (Mueller et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mueller et al., 2015.

claim: Factors that reduce microbiota diversity are associated with increased risk for diabetes mellitus.
source: Notably, factors that reduce microbiota diversity are also associated with increased risk for diabetes mellitus (Knip et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Knip et al., 2005.

claim: Loss of β cell function through autoimmunity results in abnormal glucose homeostasis and is the cause of type 1 diabetes in humans.
source: Loss of β cell function through autoimmunity results in abnormal glucose homeostasis and is the cause of type 1 diabetes (T1D) in humans.
evidence: Supported by established medical knowledge about type 1 diabetes.

claim: Decreased taxonomic diversity of the intestinal microbiota is correlated with type 1 diabetes.
source: Recent studies have shown that decreased taxonomic diversity of the intestinal microbiota is correlated with T1D (Brown et al., 2011; Giongo et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brown et al., 2011; Giongo et al., 2011.

claim: Loss of bacterial diversity precedes the onset of type 1 diabetes in children.
source: Indeed, loss of bacterial diversity precedes the onset of T1D in children, and may play a causative role in disease (Kostic et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kostic et al., 2015.

claim: Loss of bacterial diversity may play a causative role in type 1 diabetes.
source: Indeed, loss of bacterial diversity precedes the onset of T1D in children, and may play a causative role in disease (Kostic et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kostic et al., 2015 and speculative reasoning.

claim: Communication between the intestine and the pancreas is critical for overall homeostasis.
source: Communication between the intestine and the pancreas is critical for overall homeostasis.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge of digestive organ physiology.

claim: The number of β cells in conventionally reared zebrafish increased steadily from 3 to 6 dpf.
source: The number of β cells in CV fish increased steadily from 3 to 6 dpf (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The average number of β cells in germ-free zebrafish remained static from 3 to 6 dpf.
source: However, the average number of β cells in GF fish remained static over this time (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: At 6 dpf, the overall structure of β cells within the primary islet appeared much less densely packed in germ-free than in conventionally reared zebrafish.
source: Furthermore, at 6 dpf, the overall structure of β cells within the primary islet also appeared much less densely packed in GF than in CV fish (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by visual observation in Figure 1B.

claim: The total number of β cells is not different between germ-free and conventionally reared zebrafish at 3 dpf.
source: This effect is not likely to be due to changes in initial differentiation of the β cell population since the total number of β cells is not different between GF and CV fish at 3 dpf (Figure 1A), a time at which exposure to bacteria is also limited.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The amount of glucose detected in germ-free zebrafish at 6 dpf was significantly higher than in conventionally reared fish.
source: The amount of glucose detected in GF fish was significantly higher than in CV fish (Figure 1C, Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Germ-free zebrafish with a paucity of β cells are less efficient at importing and processing glucose from the blood due to lower levels of circulating insulin.
source: These data suggest that GF fish, with a paucity of β cells, are less efficient at importing and processing glucose from the blood due to lower levels of circulating insulin.
evidence: Supported by inference from glucose measurement data and established knowledge of insulin function.

claim: Free glucose levels in zebrafish larvae are correlated with β cell numbers.
source: This is consistent with previous studies showing free glucose levels in zebrafish larvae to be correlated with β cell numbers (Andersson et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Andersson et al., 2012.

claim: Addition of non-sterile, normal fish tank water to germ-free larvae at 4 dpf can rescue β cell numbers to conventionally reared levels.
source: We found that we could rescue β cell numbers to CV levels by the addition of non-sterile, normal fish tank water to GF larvae at 4 dpf (Figure 2B, Figure 2—source data 1), suggesting that development of the normal number β cells is dependent upon microbes or microbial-derived products present in the water.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Development of the normal number of β cells is dependent upon microbes or microbial-derived products present in the water.
source: We found that we could rescue β cell numbers to CV levels by the addition of non-sterile, normal fish tank water to GF larvae at 4 dpf (Figure 2B, Figure 2—source data 1), suggesting that development of the normal number β cells is dependent upon microbes or microbial-derived products present in the water.
evidence: Supported by inference from experimental data showing tank water rescue.

claim: Mono-associations with three different species of the genus Aeromonas are sufficient to rescue germ-free β cell numbers to levels observed in conventionally reared zebrafish.
source: We found that the mono-associations with three different species of the genus Aeromonas and one species of the genus Shewanella was sufficient to rescue GF β cell numbers to levels observed in CV fish (Figure 2B, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Mono-association with one species of the genus Shewanella is sufficient to rescue germ-free β cell numbers to levels observed in conventionally reared zebrafish.
source: We found that the mono-associations with three different species of the genus Aeromonas and one species of the genus Shewanella was sufficient to rescue GF β cell numbers to levels observed in CV fish (Figure 2B, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Vibrio sp. and Delftia sp. isolates are not sufficient to rescue the β cell phenotype in germ-free zebrafish.
source: Importantly, other isolates such as Vibrio sp. and Delftia sp. were not sufficient to rescue this phenotype (Figure 2B, Figure 2—source data 1), indicating that only specific members of the microbiota are capable of inducing expansion of the β cell mass.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Only specific members of the microbiota are capable of inducing expansion of the β cell mass.
source: Importantly, other isolates such as Vibrio sp. and Delftia sp. were not sufficient to rescue this phenotype (Figure 2B, Figure 2—source data 1), indicating that only specific members of the microbiota are capable of inducing expansion of the β cell mass.
evidence: Supported by inference from differential bacterial effects shown in experimental data.

claim: Cell free supernatant from each of the three strains of Aeromonas tested was able to restore β cell numbers in germ-free zebrafish.
source: For each of the three strains of Aeromonas tested, the CFS alone was able to restore β cell numbers in GF fish (Figure 3A, Figure 3—source data 1), indicating that a secreted factor (or factors) produced by these bacteria is (are) sufficient to induce β cell expansion.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A secreted factor (or factors) produced by Aeromonas bacteria is sufficient to induce β cell expansion.
source: For each of the three strains of Aeromonas tested, the CFS alone was able to restore β cell numbers in GF fish (Figure 3A, Figure 3—source data 1), indicating that a secreted factor (or factors) produced by these bacteria is (are) sufficient to induce β cell expansion.
evidence: Supported by inference from cell-free supernatant experiments.

claim: The number of β cells in fish receiving Vibrio CFS was not significantly different from that of germ-free fish.
source: We found the number of β cells in fish receiving Vibrio CFS was not significantly different from that of GF fish (Figure 3A, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The capacity to induce increased β cell numbers was lost when the Aeromonas 1 (A. veronii) CFS sample was treated with proteinase K.
source: Furthermore, the capacity to induce increased β cell numbers was lost when the Aeromonas 1 (A. veronii) CFS sample was treated with proteinase K (Figure 3A, Figure 3—source data 1), indicating that our secreted factor(s) of interest was likely to be a protein.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The secreted factor of interest from Aeromonas is likely to be a protein.
source: Furthermore, the capacity to induce increased β cell numbers was lost when the Aeromonas 1 (A. veronii) CFS sample was treated with proteinase K (Figure 3A, Figure 3—source data 1), indicating that our secreted factor(s) of interest was likely to be a protein.
evidence: Supported by inference from proteinase K treatment experiment.

claim: CFS harvested from the A. veroniiΔT2SS strain was sufficient to rescue germ-free β cell numbers.
source: Despite the fact that it has a reduced secretome, CFS harvested from the A. veroniiΔT2SS strain was sufficient to rescue GF β cell numbers (Figure 3A, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The 60–80% ammonium sulfate fraction was able to induce the greatest increase in β cell numbers.
source: Since the 60–80% fraction was able to induce the greatest increase in β cell numbers (Figure 3B), we used mass spectrometry to analyze the content of this fraction, which led to the identification of 163 proteins (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Mass spectrometry analysis of the 60–80% ammonium sulfate fraction led to the identification of 163 proteins.
source: Since the 60–80% fraction was able to induce the greatest increase in β cell numbers (Figure 3B), we used mass spectrometry to analyze the content of this fraction, which led to the identification of 163 proteins (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: The candidate gene M001_10165 is predicted to encode a putative protein of 261 amino acids.
source: Our analysis identified one single candidate gene, denoted by the locus tag, M001_10165 (10165), predicted to encode a putative protein of 261 amino acids.
evidence: Supported by bioinformatic analysis of genomic data.

claim: The putative protein encoded by M001_10165 contains a predicted N-terminal secretion sequence.
source: Consistent with the candidate protein being found in the CFS, the putative protein contained a predicted N-terminal secretion sequence.
evidence: Supported by bioinformatic prediction.

claim: Purified 10165 protein was sufficient to rescue β cell numbers to conventionally reared levels by 6 dpf.
source: Purified protein was added to flasks of 4 dpf GF zebrafish larvae. This treatment was sufficient to rescue β cell numbers to CV levels by 6 dpf (Figure 3C, Figure 3—source data 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The islets of larvae treated with the purified 10165 protein were visibly expanded compared to those of germ-free animals.
source: The islets of larvae treated with the purified protein were visibly expanded compared to those of GF animals (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by visual observation in Figure 3D.

claim: A. veroniiΔbefA shows no deficiency in in vitro growth rate compared to the wild-type strain.
source: To ensure that the loss of the befA gene would not affect the ability of A. veronii to form mono-associations with larvae, we performed growth and colonization assays and saw no deficiency in either the in vitro growth rate (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) or the ability of A. veroniiΔbefA to colonize the GF intestine compared to the wild-type (WT) strain (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A. veroniiΔbefA shows no deficiency in the ability to colonize the germ-free intestine compared to the wild-type strain.
source: To ensure that the loss of the befA gene would not affect the ability of A. veronii to form mono-associations with larvae, we performed growth and colonization assays and saw no deficiency in either the in vitro growth rate (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) or the ability of A. veroniiΔbefA to colonize the GF intestine compared to the wild-type (WT) strain (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: When inoculated in a 1:1 ratio together with A. veroniiWT, the A. veroniiΔbefA strain showed a small yet reproducible fitness disadvantage.
source: However, when inoculated in a 1:1 ratio together with A. veroniiWT, the A. veroniiΔbefA strain showed a small yet reproducible fitness disadvantage as measured by colonization level and competition index after 48 hr (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: BefA confers some colonization benefit for A. veronii within the larval gut.
source: This result indicates that BefA confers some colonization benefit for A. veronii within the larval gut.
evidence: Supported by inference from competition experiment data.

claim: Germ-free fish mono-associated with the A. veroniiΔbefA strain from 4 to 6 dpf did not have β cell numbers rescued to conventionally reared levels.
source: GF fish were mono-associated with the A. veroniiΔbefA strain, or treated with its CFS from 4 to 6 dpf. Neither treatment was sufficient to rescue β cell numbers to CV levels (Figure 4B, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Treatment with CFS from A. veroniiΔbefA was not sufficient to rescue β cell numbers to conventionally reared levels.
source: GF fish were mono-associated with the A. veroniiΔbefA strain, or treated with its CFS from 4 to 6 dpf. Neither treatment was sufficient to rescue β cell numbers to CV levels (Figure 4B, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Mono-associations of A. veroniiΔbefA could be complemented in trans with either CFS from A. veroniiWT or purified BefA protein, resulting in the restoration of the β cell population.
source: However, mono-associations of A. veroniiΔbefA could be complemented in trans with either CFS from A. veroniiWT or purified BefA protein, which resulted in the restoration of the β cell population (Figure 4B, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The BefA protein is necessary in an A. veronii mono-association for early β cell expansion.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that the BefA protein is necessary in an A. veronii mono-association for early β cell expansion and suggests that A. veronii only produces a single effector of host β cell expansion.
evidence: Supported by inference from mutant complementation experiments.

claim: A. veronii only produces a single effector of host β cell expansion.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that the BefA protein is necessary in an A. veronii mono-association for early β cell expansion and suggests that A. veronii only produces a single effector of host β cell expansion.
evidence: Supported by inference from complementation experiments showing BefA is sufficient.

claim: Proliferation is the primary mode of human neonatal β cell expansion.
source: Proliferation is the primary mode of human neonatal β cell expansion (Gregg et al., 2012; Kassem et al., 2000; Teta et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gregg et al., 2012; Kassem et al., 2000; Teta et al., 2007.

claim: In 4–6 dpf zebrafish larvae, proliferation contributes to β cell expansion.
source: In 4–6 dpf zebrafish larvae, proliferation also contributes to β cell expansion (Field et al., 2003; Hesselson et al., 2009; Moro et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Field et al., 2003; Hesselson et al., 2009; Moro et al., 2009.

claim: By 6 dpf, conventionally reared larvae had significantly more EdU labeled insulin-expressing cells than germ-free larvae.
source: We found that, by 6 dpf, CV larvae had significantly more EdU labeled insulin-expressing cells than GF larvae (Figure 5A,B, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Treatment of germ-free larvae with BefA was sufficient to restore β cell proliferation to conventionally reared levels.
source: Next we asked whether treatment of GF larvae with BefA was sufficient to restore β cell proliferation to CV levels. We found that BefA-treated GF larvae had EdU incorporation similar to CV fish and significantly greater than GF (Figure 5A,B, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: CFS from A. veroniiΔbefA strain was not sufficient to increase proliferation rates in germ-free fish.
source: CFS from our A. veroniiΔbefA strain was not sufficient to increase proliferation rates in GF fish (Figure 5B, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: BefA is sufficient to increase cell proliferation that gives rise to an expanded β cell population during early larval development.
source: Our results show that BefA is sufficient to increase cell proliferation that gives rise to an expanded β cell population during early larval development.
evidence: Supported by inference from EdU incorporation experiments.

claim: BefA is the only product of the A. veronii CFS that is capable of inducing β cell proliferation.
source: Furthermore, BefA seems to be the only product of the A. veronii CFS that is capable of inducing this cell proliferation.
evidence: Supported by inference from mutant CFS experiments showing no proliferation effect.

claim: Both the proliferation of existing β cells and the proliferation of progenitors contribute to the expansion of β cells that occurs between 4 and 6 dpf in zebrafish larvae.
source: In zebrafish larvae, both the proliferation of existing β cells as well as the proliferation of progenitors contribute to the expansion of β cells that occurs between 4 and 6 dpf (Dong et al., 2007; Field et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dong et al., 2007; Field et al., 2003.

claim: Neogenesis of β cells from progenitors can be detected as the appearance of insulin positive cells in the extra-pancreatic duct.
source: Neogenesis of β cells from progenitors is also rare, but can be detected as the appearance of insulin positive cells in the extra-pancreatic duct (EPD) (Dong et al., 2007; Hesselson et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dong et al., 2007; Hesselson et al., 2009.

claim: There is a slight but significant increase in EPD-localized insulin expressing cells in conventionally reared versus germ-free fish at 6 dpf.
source: In a survey of over 500 Tg(-1.0insulin:eGFP) larvae, we found a slight but significant increase in EPD-localized insulin expressing cells in CV versus GF fish (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the microbiota increases endocrine progenitor proliferation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The microbiota increases endocrine progenitor proliferation.
source: In a survey of over 500 Tg(-1.0insulin:eGFP) larvae, we found a slight but significant increase in EPD-localized insulin expressing cells in CV versus GF fish (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the microbiota increases endocrine progenitor proliferation.
evidence: Supported by inference from EPD insulin-positive cell counts.

claim: There is no difference in the level of exocrine cell proliferation across germ-free, conventionally reared and BefA treatments.
source: We found no difference in the level of exocrine cell proliferation across GF, CV and BefA treatments (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: There is no difference in the total numbers of glucagon-expressing α cells across germ-free, conventionally reared and BefA treated fish.
source: To test whether β cells were the only endocrine cell type in the islet to be responsive to BefA, we also quantified the total number of glucagon-expressing α (Figure 5D) and somatostatin-expressing δ (Figure 5E) cells in GF, CV and BefA treated fish. We again found no difference in the total numbers of these cells across treatments (Figure 5F,G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D,F.

claim: There is no difference in the total numbers of somatostatin-expressing δ cells across germ-free, conventionally reared and BefA treated fish.
source: To test whether β cells were the only endocrine cell type in the islet to be responsive to BefA, we also quantified the total number of glucagon-expressing α (Figure 5D) and somatostatin-expressing δ (Figure 5E) cells in GF, CV and BefA treated fish. We again found no difference in the total numbers of these cells across treatments (Figure 5F,G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E,G.

claim: In the pancreas, β cells alone are responsive to the presence of BefA.
source: These results suggest that in the pancreas, β cells alone are responsive to the presence of BefA.
evidence: Supported by inference from cell type-specific proliferation experiments.

claim: Close homologs of BefA (at least 82% amino acid sequence identity) are found in many, but not all, species of the Aeromonas, Vibrio, and Photobacterium genera.
source: Phylogenetic analysis of related sequences in bacterial genomes uncovered close homologs (at least 82% amino acid sequence identity) in many, but not all, species of the Aeromonas, Vibrio, and Photobacterium genera.
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis data.

claim: A highly related BefA sequence in the human-associated species Enterococcus gallinarum was likely acquired through a horizontal gene transfer event.
source: We also found an example of a highly related sequence in the human-associated species Enterococcus gallinarum, which was likely acquired through a horizontal gene transfer event (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: More distant BefA homologs are found in three additional human-associated genera: Enterobacter, Escherichia, and Klebsiella.
source: Widening the search to include more distant homologs identified potentially related genes in three additional human-associated genera: Enterobacter, Escherichia, and Klebsiella (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The Enterococcus gallinarum BefA homolog can rescue β cell numbers to conventionally reared levels in germ-free zebrafish.
source: Upon addition of these supernatants to GF larval zebrafish, we observed rescue of β cell numbers to the CV level with both the Enterococcus gallinarum and Enterobacter aerogenes proteins, but not the empty vector control (Figure 6D, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Members of human-associated microbiota produce secreted proteins capable of inducing β cell expansion.

claim: BefA and related homologues are predicted to contain a C-terminal SYLF domain.

evidence: Supported by bioinformatic prediction and citation to Hasegawa et al., 2011.

claim: Type 1 diabetes is caused by both genetic and environmental factors.

claim: There is 50% disease discordance for type 1 diabetes among monozygotic twins.

claim: Microbiota composition is an environmental factor associated with type 1 diabetes.

claim: Multiple aspects of host immune cell development and function known to play a role in type 1 diabetes are altered by the loss of microbes.

claim: The early microbiota may play a role in establishing the β cell population size that would either buffer against, or render individuals susceptible to, β cell depletion by autoimmune destruction.

evidence: Supported by speculative reasoning based on experimental findings.

claim: Human β cells undergo a period of postnatal expansion before becoming quiescent around age two.
source: In humans, β cells undergo a period of postnatal expansion, before becoming quiescent around age two (Gregg et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gregg et al., 2012.

claim: Differences in β cell growth during early postnatal life account for the wide variation in β cell mass observed in adults.
source: Differences in β cell growth during this time are thought to account for the wide variation in β cell mass observed in adults (Wang et al., 2015b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2015b.

claim: Early life β cell census could influence diabetes risk.
source: The idea that early life β cell census could influence diabetes risk is supported by studies in both rodents and humans, and has been theorized as an important risk factor for type 2 diabetes (Kaijser et al., 2009), a disease which is also influenced strongly by microbiota composition (Cox and Blaser, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kaijser et al., 2009 and Cox and Blaser, 2014.

claim: Type 2 diabetes is influenced strongly by microbiota composition.
source: The idea that early life β cell census could influence diabetes risk is supported by studies in both rodents and humans, and has been theorized as an important risk factor for type 2 diabetes (Kaijser et al., 2009), a disease which is also influenced strongly by microbiota composition (Cox and Blaser, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cox and Blaser, 2014.

claim: Compromised β cell development in rats results in an insufficient number of cells to adequately control glucose metabolism.
source: Compromised β cell development in rats results in an insufficient number of cells to adequately control glucose metabolism (Figliuzzi et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Figliuzzi et al., 2010.

claim: In mice, perinatal β cell proliferation rates can be tuned via the modulation of Gi-GPCR signaling.
source: In mice, perinatal β cell proliferation rates can be tuned via the modulation of Gi-GPCR signaling (Berger et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Berger et al., 2015.

claim: Changes to early β cell proliferation capacity in mice correlates directly with adult β cell mass, which subsequently impacts glucose regulation.
source: Changes to early β cell proliferation capacity in these mice correlates directly with adult β cell mass, which subsequently impacts glucose regulation (Berger et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Berger et al., 2015.

claim: Meta analysis of human data has revealed a correlation between an early age of β cell loss and more rapid onset of type 1 diabetes.
source: Furthermore, meta analysis of human data has revealed a correlation between an early age of β cell loss and more rapid onset of T1D (Klinke, 2008), consistent with the model that failure to generate a reserve of β cells early in development increases disease risk.
evidence: Supported by citation to Klinke, 2008.

claim: Failure to generate a reserve of β cells early in development increases type 1 diabetes disease risk.
source: Furthermore, meta analysis of human data has revealed a correlation between an early age of β cell loss and more rapid onset of T1D (Klinke, 2008), consistent with the model that failure to generate a reserve of β cells early in development increases disease risk.
evidence: Supported by inference from cited meta-analysis and speculative reasoning.

claim: Neonatal microbiomes with a low abundance of BefA equivalents would result in reduced β cell proliferation, lower β cell mass, and increased diabetes risk.

evidence: Supported by speculative reasoning based on experimental findings.

claim: Specific bacterial lineages have been shown to attenuate disease in diabetes models, including Segmented Filamentous Bacteria (SFB) in the non-obese diabetic (NOD) mouse.
source: For example, specific bacterial lineages have been shown to attenuate disease in diabetes models, including Segmented Filamentous Bacteria (SFB) in the non-obese diabetic (NOD) mouse (Kriegel et al., 2011; Yurkovetskiy et al., 2013) and Lactobacillus johnsonii in the Biobreeding rat model (Valladares et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kriegel et al., 2011; Yurkovetskiy et al., 2013.

claim: Lactobacillus johnsonii attenuates disease in the Biobreeding rat diabetes model.

claim: Certain microbial assemblages, but not others, confer disease protection in neonatal NOD mice.

evidence: Supported by citation to Peng et al., 2014.

claim: Early development is a critical window for microbiota modulation of disease risk in NOD mice.
source: Additional recent work by Wen and colleagues demonstrates early development as a critical window for microbiota modulation of disease risk in NOD mice (Hu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hu et al., 2015.

claim: BefA acts during early developmental stages in zebrafish.
source: We have shown that BefA acts during early developmental stages in zebrafish, and we hypothesize that β cell expansion during this developmental window is important for disease prevention, and may be a critical period for clinical intervention for infants at risk for T1D development.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing BefA effects in early larval stages.

claim: β cell expansion during early developmental stages may be important for disease prevention.
source: We have shown that BefA acts during early developmental stages in zebrafish, and we hypothesize that β cell expansion during this developmental window is important for disease prevention, and may be a critical period for clinical intervention for infants at risk for T1D development.
evidence: Supported by speculative reasoning based on experimental findings.

claim: Early development may be a critical period for clinical intervention for infants at risk for type 1 diabetes development.
source: We have shown that BefA acts during early developmental stages in zebrafish, and we hypothesize that β cell expansion during this developmental window is important for disease prevention, and may be a critical period for clinical intervention for infants at risk for T1D development.
evidence: Supported by speculative reasoning based on experimental findings and cited literature.

claim: BefA confers a slight colonization advantage to A. veronii in the context of co-colonization with wild type A. veronii.
source: In the context of the zebrafish intestinal environment, BefA confers a slight colonization advantage to A. veronii, however this is unlikely to be related to its capacity to induce β cell mass, because the colonization requirement is only apparent in the context of co-colonization with wild type A. veronii that induce normal β cell numbers.
evidence: Supported by inference from competition experiments.

claim: Bacteria may produce BefA for a purpose independent of β cell expansion and the host simply uses this bacterial molecule as a cue for its own developmental program.

evidence: Supported by speculative reasoning about evolutionary function.

claim: The incidence of autoimmune diseases such as type 1 diabetes has been increasing markedly in developed nations over the past several decades.

evidence: Supported by established epidemiological knowledge.

claim: The disappearing microbiota hypothesis proposes that as modern lifestyles have become increasingly sterile, we have lost ancestral microbial symbionts important for specific aspects of our health.
source: One theory to explain this phenomenon is the disappearing microbiota hypothesis, which proposes that over time, as our modern lifestyles have become increasingly sterile, we have lost ancestral microbial symbionts important for specific aspects of our health (Blaser and Falkow, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Blaser and Falkow, 2009.

claim: Loss of specific microbial taxa from gut microbiota could underlie increased diabetes risk.
source: Our discovery of a specific class of bacterial proteins that promote β cell expansion in early development is consistent with the hypothesis that loss of specific microbial taxa from gut microbiota could underlie increased diabetes risk.
evidence: Supported by inference from experimental findings and speculative reasoning.

claim: BefA-like proteins promote the establishment of a robust β cell population that is more resilient to subsequent β cell loss.
source: Specifically, we suggest that BefA-like proteins promote the establishment of a robust β cell population that is more resilient to subsequent β cell loss.
evidence: Supported by speculative reasoning based on experimental findings.

evidence: Supported by citations to Andersson et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2015a.
